old_entry.title: Contra
old_entry.summary: Contra is a 1987 run and gun video game developed and published by Konami for arcades.
body: Contra is a 1987 run and gun video game developed and published by Konami for arcades. A home version was released for the Nintendo Entertainment System in 1988, along with ports for various home computer formats, including the MSX2. The arcade and computer versions were localized as Gryzor in Europe, and the NES version as Probotector in the PAL region.

The arcade game was a commercial success worldwide, becoming one of the top four highest-grossing dedicated arcade games of 1987 in the United States. The NES version was also a critical and commercial success, with Electronic Gaming Monthly awarding it for being the Best Action Game of 1988. Several Contra sequels were produced following the original game.

Contra employs a variety of playing perspectives, which include a standard side view, a pseudo-3D view (in which the player proceeds by shooting and moving towards the background, in addition to left or right) and a fixed screen format (in which the player has their gun aimed upwards by default). Up to two people can play simultaneously, with one player as Bill (the blond-haired commando wearing a white tank top and blue bandana), and the other player as Lance (the shirtless dark-haired commando with a red bandana).

The controls consist of an eight-way joystick and two action buttons for shooting (left) and jumping (right). When one of the protagonists jumps, he curls into a somersault instead of doing a conventional jump like in other games. The joystick controls not only the player's movement while running and jumping, but also his aiming. During side view stages, the player can shoot leftward, rightward or upward while standing, as well as horizontally and diagonally while running. The player can also shoot in any of eight directions, including downwards, while jumping. Pressing the joystick downwards while standing will cause the character to lie down on his stomach, allowing him to avoid enemy fire and shoot low targets. When the jump button is pressed while crouching on a higher platform, the character will drop down to a lower level.

The player's default weapon is a rifle with unlimited ammunition that can be upgraded into one of four other guns. These can be obtained by destroying the pill box sensors and flying item capsules containing them, or by defeating the red-clad guards in the enemy bases. These consist of a machine gun that fires rapidly when the fire button is held down, a laser gun that shoots a powerful beam, a fireball gun that shoots its rounds in a corkscrew pattern, and a shotgun that shoots five individual bullets in individual directions. There are also two auxiliary power-ups that only appear in certain areas when the character is armed: a rapid-bullets upgrade that increases the firing speed of the gun's shots and a barrier that makes the character invulnerable for a limited period. With the exception of the machine gun and the laser gun, each item comes in the form of a Falcon-shaped symbol marked with a letter representing its function (F, S, R and B). Though in the home versions of the game, machine gun and laser gun also come in the form of a Falcon-shaped symbol marked with a letter representing its function (M and L respectively).

The player loses a life if their character (Bill or Lance) comes into contact with enemies or their missiles, fails to complete a base stage before the time limit, or falls into a bottomless pit. When that happens, the character will revert to his default weapon on his next life. After losing all lives, the player can continue by inserting more coins (if necessary) and pressing Start, but only up to three times. A second player can join in anytime, but if one player loses all of their lives, they must wait until the other player loses their lives as well to continue together.

The arcade version of Contra consists of seven stages (the number of stages and level structures vary in later versions). The first stage is a side-scrolling level where the player character is dropped into the jungle and must fend off the enemy's initial line of defense until he reaches the entrance of the first base, where he must destroy a large sensor to enter the base. The game switches to a 3D view for the second stage, where the player character must fight his way through a series of passageways inside the base before time runs out (a display at the top of the screen shows the map of the base and the time remaining). The player must destroy a generator at the other side of each passageway in order to deactivate the electric current preventing access. The third stage is set in the core of the base in a fixed screen, where the player must destroy the enemy's defense system in order to expose the final target, a giant eyeball that shoots fireballs.

old_entry.title: Dragon Quest II
old_entry.summary: Dragon Quest II: Luminaries of the Legendary Line, titled Dragon Warrior II when initially localized to North America, is a 1987 role-playing video game developed by Chunsoft and published by Enix for the Nintendo Entertainment System as a part of the Dragon Quest series.
body: Dragon Quest II: Luminaries of the Legendary Line, titled Dragon Warrior II when initially localized to North America, is a 1987 role-playing video game developed by Chunsoft and published by Enix for the Nintendo Entertainment System as a part of the Dragon Quest series.  Enix's U.S. subsidiary published the American release, Dragon Warrior II, for the Nintendo Entertainment System in 1990. Dragon Quest II is set one hundred years after the events of the first game.

The game's story centers on the prince of Midenhall, who is ordered to stop an evil wizard named Hargon after Hargon destroys Moonbrooke Castle. On his adventure, he is accompanied by his two cousins, the prince of Cannock and the princess of Moonbrooke (and the princess of Cannock in Dragon Quest I & II HD-2D Remake). Dragon Quest II expands on the first game by having a larger party, more areas to explore, multiple heroes and enemies in a battle, and a sailing ship. The game's successor, Dragon Quest III, follows the ancestor of the main characters, the legendary hero Erdrick; and the three games are collectively called "The Erdrick Trilogy".

Planning began a month before the original Dragon Quest was released. One major goal was the development of a more exciting combat system, which was inspired by similar multi-character party systems such as the one found in Wizardry. The artwork that was used as the basis for the characters and monsters was painted by Akira Toriyama and then translated into pixel art. The game was hit with delays due to game balance, which were only fully corrected in the early sections of the game. This, combined with a staff that included students not familiar with the coding and debugging process, pushed back the release by a month. The developers also had many ideas that had to be discarded due to the technical limitations of the Famicom system, though some were later incorporated into subsequent remakes and the game's sequel, Dragon Quest III.

Dragon Quest II was successful in Japan; the original Famicom version shipped over 2.4 million copies. Later, the game was remade for the Super Famicom and the Game Boy Color and combined with the original Dragon Quest game in a release entitled Dragon Quest I & II. A version of the game for Android and iOS was released in Japan on June 26, 2014, and worldwide on October 9, 2014, as Dragon Quest II: Luminaries of the Legendary Line.  The game was praised for improving on almost all aspects of the original, including having better graphics, having a larger world to explore, and more characters to participate in a more dynamic combat system.

Dragon Quest II is known as one of the most difficult Dragon Quest games, especially in its late game, and retained that reputation even in later ports to other platforms that made the game somewhat more forgiving.

old_entry.title: Yume Kōjō: Doki Doki Panic
old_entry.subtitle: Doki Doki Panic Shows How a Game Can Change Identity Without Losing Its Rules
old_entry.summary: On July 10, 1987 Fuji TV released Yume Kōjō: Doki Doki Panic, developed by Nintendo for the Famicom Disk System.
body: On July 10, 1987 Fuji TV released Yume Kōjō: Doki Doki Panic, developed by Nintendo for the Famicom Disk System. The platformer was tied to the Yume Kōjō '87 event and introduced four protagonists with different abilities, objects pulled from the ground and enemies that could be thrown. Soon afterward, the same structure was reworked for Western markets as Super Mario Bros. 2. Its history exposes a rare process: characters, framing and brand change while many of the rules remain strong enough to support a second identity.

The title Yume Kōjō: Doki Doki Panic is derived from "doki doki", a Japanese onomatopoeia for the sound of a quickly beating heart. The title and character concept were inspired by a license cooperation between Nintendo and Fuji Television to promote the broadcaster's Yume Kōjō '87 event, which showcased several of its latest TV shows and consumer products. The Yume Kōjō festival's mascots became the game's protagonists: a family consisting of the boy Imajin, his girlfriend Lina, and his parents Mama and Papa. The rest of the game's characters, including the main villain named Mamu, were created by Nintendo for the project. Yume Kōjō: Doki Doki Panic takes place within a book with an Arabian setting. All four characters are optionally playable, though the game is not fully completed until the player clears all levels using each protagonist.

The conception of a third Super Mario installment began shortly after the release of The Legend of Zelda in February 1986. An early prototype with vertical scrolling was developed in two months by Kensuke Tanabe, designed by a team led by Shigeru Miyamoto, and programmed by Nintendo's frequent partner, SRD. The first prototype's gameplay emphasizes vertically scrolling levels with two-player cooperative action: lifting, carrying, and throwing each other; lifting, carrying, throwing, stacking, and climbing objects; and incrementally scrolling the screen upward when reaching the top. Dissatisfied so far, Miyamoto then added the traditional horizontal scrolling, saying to "make something a little bit more Mario-like", and saying "Maybe we need to change this up ... As long as it's fun, anything goes". The prototype software was too complex for Famicom hardware at the time, and the gameplay was still considered lacking, especially in single-player mode.

For the international conversion into Super Mario Bros. 2, many graphical changes were made to the scenery and characters' look, animation, and identity. The R&D4 staff modified the character likenesses of Mario, Luigi, Princess Toadstool, and Toad, building them over their respective counterpart models of Imajin, Mama, Lina, and Papa. This marked the first time that Mario and Luigi had noticeably different heights, and Miyamoto originated the scuttling animation of Luigi's legs, to justify the enhanced jumping ability seen in the corresponding Mama character. Yume Kōjō: Doki Doki Panic needed only a few alterations for its conversion into the Mario series because its gameplay elements were already so heavily rooted in it: Starman for invincibility, the sound effects of coins and jumps, POW blocks, warp zones, and a soundtrack by Super Mario Bros. composer Koji Kondo. To reduce the game's overall difficulty, the designers made minor technical changes. They opted not to retain Yume Kōjō: Doki Doki Panic's ultimate requirement to complete each level using each protagonist; therefore, this new Super Mario Bros. 2 can be completed in only one pass by any combination of characters. A late prototype of the game covering these changes was exhibited in the first issue of Nintendo Power, dated July/August 1988. In the tradition of the Mario series, they added the ability to run by holding the B button.

original.old_heading: Four protagonists change how the level is read
original.old_body: The four characters differ in jumping, strength and behavior, so the same space gains different values depending on who is chosen and the initial selection becomes part of strategy. Writing does not remain separate from the rules. Goals, characters and transformations gain weight because players encounter them through actions, constraints and consequences, not only during narrative scenes. Story organizes the experience while the system gives the story concrete form. It is a difficult balance: when it works, a plot development also changes how a battle, a space or a choice is read. The work's memory then grows from the connection between what is told and what the player is asked to do.

original.old_heading: Pulling and throwing replace jumping as the only answer
original.old_body: Vegetables, blocks and enemies can be lifted and thrown, creating a different physical logic from the classic Mario platformer and turning the environment into a reserve of offensive tools. The mechanic does not live in isolation: it changes the value of space, time and resources, forcing players to build priorities while the situation changes. The result remains readable because the rule produces observable consequences rather than only hidden numbers. That relationship between a local decision and the rhythm of the whole play session is what makes the system memorable. Looking at it today shows how the game turns a simple idea into a grammar learned through attempts, mistakes and anticipation.

As long as it's fun, anything goes". The prototype software was too complex for Famicom hardware at the time, and the gameplay was still considered lacking, especially in single-player mode.

original.old_heading: From television event to Super Mario Bros. 2
original.old_body: The later replacement of characters and adaptation for Western markets show how a gameplay structure can be reused, reinterpreted and inserted into another series without disappearing. The choice needs to be read within the technical and production constraints of its period. Memory, processors, storage, peripherals and pipelines are not neutral background details: they define what can be shown and therefore what can become interaction. A project gains identity when it turns a limitation or capability of the hardware into a recognizable rule. Technology matters here less as a specification list than as a method, making visible the passage from an available tool to a form of play that would previously have been harder to build.
original.heading: How Nintendo converted Doki Doki Panic into Mario
original.body: For the international conversion into Super Mario Bros. 2, many graphical changes were made to the scenery and characters' look, animation, and identity. The R&D4 staff modified the character likenesses of Mario, Luigi, Princess Toadstool, and Toad, building them over their respective counterpart models of Imajin, Mama, Lina, and Papa. This marked the first time that Mario and Luigi had noticeably different heights, and Miyamoto originated the scuttling animation of Luigi's legs, to justify the enhanced jumping ability seen in the corresponding Mama character. Yume Kōjō: Doki Doki Panic needed only a few alterations for its conversion into the Mario series because its gameplay elements were already so heavily rooted in it: Starman for invincibility, the sound effects of coins and jumps, POW blocks, warp zones, and a soundtrack by Super Mario Bros. composer Koji Kondo. To reduce the game's overall difficulty, the designers made minor technical changes. They opted not to retain Yume Kōjō: Doki Doki Panic's ultimate requirement to complete each level using each protagonist; therefore, this new Super Mario Bros. 2 can be completed in only one pass by any combination of characters. A late prototype of the game covering these changes was exhibited in the first issue of Nintendo Power, dated July/August 1988. In the tradition of the Mario series, they added the ability to run by holding the B button.

old_entry.title: Phantasy Star
old_entry.subtitle: The sword meets the spaceport
old_entry.summary: On December 20, 1987, SEGA released Phantasy Star in Japan for Mark III and Master System.
body: On December 20, 1987, SEGA released Phantasy Star in Japan for Mark III and Master System. The project was conceived as both a personal and technological response to role-playing games of the era: Reiko Kodama recalls a team deliberately looking for different solutions, from protagonist Alis to first-person three-dimensional dungeons and animated enemies in battle. The setting mixes swords, magic, robots, spaceships and three planets of the Algol Solar System, moving fantasy beyond its customary imaginary Middle Ages. FM support also adds particular sonic richness on compatible configurations. Phantasy Star therefore does more than transfer an RPG onto SEGA hardware: it uses technical features and art direction to define a colorful science fiction world where exploration can move from a village to a three-dimensional corridor and then to interplanetary travel.

Reiko Kodama, designer of the first Phantasy Star, recalled that the team worked with almost no internal RPG tradition and often tried to do the opposite of what it saw elsewhere. In that context Alis took shape, a fifteen-year-old girl who sets out to avenge her brother and becomes the center of the adventure. Kodama remembers drawing numerous versions of her and trying to preserve a recognizable femininity without reducing her to passivity. The choice should not be turned into a false claim of absolute precedence, but it remains significant in the landscape of 1987 console role-playing games, dominated by male protagonists or minimally characterized parties. Alis leads the group and drives the plot through a personal motivation. The character thus becomes a statement of tone before being a statistical function.

SEGA identifies the moving three-dimensional dungeons as one of the first Phantasy Star's most technologically striking features. Entering a cave or tower shifts the perspective from a top-down view to first-person corridors that have to be memorized as sequences of turns, doors and intersections. Kodama recalls that the team deliberately chose this solution precisely because it was uncommon in the console role-playing games it observed. The change of perspective is not merely spectacle: it alters the ability to orient oneself. The map cannot be read all at once, and the player has to build it mentally, accepting the possibility of getting lost. Modern reissues have added automapping tools precisely to reduce this difficulty. In the original, technology instead becomes a form of controlled disorientation that immediately distinguishes underground exploration from travel on the surface.

Phantasy Star sets its adventure across Palma, Motavia and Dezoris, three planets with different environments and obstacles. SEGA documentation describes spaceports, passports, shuttles and specialized vehicles that allow players to cross sand, water or walls of ice. This structure makes science fiction part of the exploration system. Simply changing the backdrop is not enough to declare that the player is on another planet: available routes, services, creatures and necessary tools also change. The Land Master crosses difficult desert areas, the Flow Mover travels over water and rivers, and the Ice Digger opens passages through ice. Progress is therefore also measured by the ability to move through environments that were previously inaccessible. The presence of a spaceship and ground vehicles places fantasy logic and technology in the same inventory, making natural a combination that still seemed unusual in 1987.

SEGA recalls that Phantasy Star also tried to distinguish itself in presentation: enemies animate their attacks in battle and, on compatible configurations, the music uses the FM unit. Kodama has said that the team wanted to avoid the immobility typical of many enemies in contemporary role-playing games and bring into the genre experience SEGA had gained through action games. Even the two-dimensional maps were designed with moving elements such as water and walkways. This attention produces a world that seems less static while still being bound to 8-bit hardware. Animation alone does not change the rules of combat, but it changes how the player perceives the enemy and the response to an attack. Likewise, the FM timbre does not add content, but gives the science fiction setting a sonic quality different from the more traditional repertoire of console fantasy.

old_entry.title: Digital Devil Story: Megami Tensei
old_entry.subtitle: The Monster Can Change Sides
old_entry.summary: On September 11, 1987, Namco released Digital Devil Story: Megami Tensei for Famicom in Japan, developed by Atlus from the universe of Aya Nishitani's novels.
body: On September 11, 1987, Namco released Digital Devil Story: Megami Tensei for Famicom in Japan, developed by Atlus from the universe of Aya Nishitani's novels. It is a first-person dungeon RPG, but its legacy depends on more than labyrinthine corridors. The game already introduces ideas that would become central to Megami Tensei and, later, Shin Megami Tensei: demons can be fought, persuaded to join the party and fused to create new creatures. The opponent therefore stops being a fixed category. It can become a resource, a companion or material for a later transformation. In the context of the Famicom in 1987, this structure combines demanding exploration, party management and experimentation, making knowledge of the bestiary as important to progression as gaining levels.

Digital Devil Story: Megami Tensei builds much of its adventure inside labyrinths viewed from a first-person perspective. The corridor ahead reveals little of the overall route, so finding one's way requires memory, note-taking and attention to turns, stairs and doors. Difficulty does not come only from the demons encountered: getting lost means consuming time and resources before combat even begins. This form of exploration turns knowledge of space into invisible equipment. Every return makes a section easier to read and reduces uncertainty, while a detour can reveal either a shortcut or a new risk. The dungeon is therefore not a neutral container for random encounters. It is a system that tests the ability to build a mental representation while the screen provides information only locally.

One of the game's decisive ideas is allowing a hostile demon to become an ally. Instead of treating every encounter as a question with only one answer, Megami Tensei opens a space for negotiation in which the player can try to persuade the creature to join the party. The idea grew from the creators' interest in tabletop role-playing and in the possibility of speaking with something that would normally be classified only as an enemy. The systemic consequence is profound. An opponent is no longer valuable exclusively for the experience earned by defeating it: it has abilities, affinities and future potential within the team. Conversation does not remove risk or make demons docile; it adds another form of reading, turning the bestiary into a network of possible relationships.

Demon fusion introduces a logic of growth different from simple accumulation. Two useful creatures can be sacrificed to obtain a new one, forcing the player to weigh present value against future possibilities. A demon matters not only for what it can do in battle: it can become an ingredient in a combination better suited to later dungeons. This rule turns party composition into a form of continuous design. Recruitment, combat and fusion feed into one another because encountering new creatures expands the vocabulary from which the team can be built. The system would be refined across many later entries, but the principle is already recognizable in 1987. Megami Tensei turns collection into transformation: progressing means learning when to keep an ally and when to convert its value into something that does not yet exist.
